made a drive to within fifty miles of Angora. Then Kemal, in a vigorous campaign in the fall of 1922, utterly routed the Greek invaders and thrust them out of Asia Minor. This victory was followed by the deposition of the sultan, and the whole Turkish nation was thereby brought under the rule of the new republican government at Angora. 

When Kemal advanced to seize Constantinople a clash seemed imminent with the British forces guarding the Straits. The 

Allies, however, at last drew together and forced the Turks to agree to a peace conference at Lausanne, in Switzerland. The sessions of this conference were long and stormy, but in July, 1923, a treaty was finally signed, recognizing the new Turkish

state, but with important modifications of its old-time boundaries. Turkey was given full sovereignty over Constantinople, the 

Zone of the Straits, eastern Thrace, and all of Asia Minor, but surrendered her authority over all territory beyond these limits. 

Greeks were to be removed from Turkey and Turks from Greek territory, while the waterway between the Ægean and the Black Sea was to be kept free for the ships of all nations. Thus Turkey under the Kemalists recovered her place of importance as ruler of Constantinople and Asia Minor, though her old supremacy over Arabia, Mesopotamia, Syria, and Palestine was lost. 

THE NEW PARLIAMENT BUILDING OF THE TURKISH REPUBLIC AT ANGORA Turkey Adopts Western Ideas. The Turkish nationalists are attempting to strengthen their new republic by adopting the habits and customs of western Europe. In addition to establishing a parliamentary form of government they have adopted a modern system of law borrowed from the laws of Switzerland, Italy, and Germany. They have legally abolished slavery and polygamy and have freed women from the seclusion of the harem. They are trying to force both men and women to wear western styles of clothing. Education is being promoted, a new university has been founded at Constantinople, and, in 1928,

RUSSIA UNDER THE BOLSHEVIKI 

797 the Latin alphabet was substituted for the peculiar Turkish alphabets hitherto used to write the various Turkish dialects. 

Thus a most interesting attempt is being made in the Near East to substitute modern ways of life and thought for the centuriesold despotism and stagnation of Oriental life. 

RUSSIA UNDER THE BOLSHEVIKI 

- After the 

66 Red "Régime in Russia Causes Alarm Outside. treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Russia took no more part in the World War against Germany, and had no share in making the general peace treaties. The Bolshevik authorities displayed an aggressive, crusading attitude toward the outside world, aiming to extend afar the supposed blessings of the Russian brand of extreme socialism. For this reason most outside nations were either cold or hostile toward soviet Russia. The Bolshevik government was for some time denied official and legal recognition by other nations. Gradually, however, between 1922 and 

1925, Germany, Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan gave her recognition. The United States for years held Russia an outlaw among the nations, because, as Secretary of State Hughes said in 1923, she still held to revolutionary aims toward other governments, and because she failed to protect the lives and property of foreigners. Ten years later, however, in 

November, 1933, President Franklin D. Roosevelt recognized the Russian government.

Bolshevism in Russia an Inverted Régime. - Meanwhile, within soviet Russia the radical principles of the Bolsheviki were being applied energetically. Reacting from the czarist régime which bitterly oppressed the masses, the new masters of Russia sought desperately to set up an inverted social order. 

Everything was to yield to the dominance of the workingman. 

Property, both real and personal, including that of foreigners, was confiscated and socialized. 

Labor in the socialized industries and on public works was conscripted - no class or profession being exempt. When the crops of the peasants were likewise requisitioned at govern-

ment prices, the peasants naturally quit raising anything for sale. Scarcity of food and of other necessities became acute. 

Under these conditions farming as well as manufacturing declined, and the industrial life of the nation was well-nigh extinguished. 

Not a Real Democracy. - Politically, there was no effort to learn the wishes of the whole people or to establish a real democratic government. The local soviets of laborers and soldiers were represented in the All-Russian Congress of Soviets, which, in turn, chose the central executive committee to supervise the working of the government. This executive committee appointed the council of people's commissaries, eighteen in number, of which Lenin was president, until his death in 1924, and Trotsky for a time was commissary of war. 

While all citizens engaged in productive labor were entitled to vote for the local soviets, yet the elections were a sham. By a complicated system of indirect elections, the actual rulers of the state were far removed from popular control, and they were thus not directly responsible to any one. The entire system was dominated by the aggressive revolutionary leaders at Moscow, the new capital, who frequently nominated the candidates and by terrorist methods secured their election. 

To maintain itself in power, the soviet government was utterly intolerant of opposition, just as was the first French Republic in the midst of its famous Reign of Terror; and the Bolsheviki, in their methods of repression, much resembled the men of 1793 and 1794 in France. Although there was supposed to be complete personal liberty in Russia, yet freedom of speech and of the press existed only for upholders of the soviet system. 

Persons suspected of counter-revolutionary aims were dealt with rigorously. The fact that a man had been an employer of labor, a capitalist, a bourgeois, or an intellectual, caused him to be suspected of hostility to the revolution. Executions and deportations of unwelcome persons, especially during the first three or four years of the revolution, were shockingly frequent. 

How many victims there were it is difficult to say because of the

RUSSIA UNDER THE BOLSHEVIKI 

799 meagerness of exact information coming from Russia since 1917. 

In 1922 a Paris newspaper, claiming to quote an official soviet report, stated that the number of persons executed had been over 1,750,000, almost half being peasants, and over 15,000 being doctors and teachers. This seems impossible of belief. Yet it is certain that the Bolshevik leaders were ruthless in the war against their opponents.

The Union of Socialist Soviet Republics (U.S.S.R.). — By military force and political agitation the Bolsheviki - soon taking the name Communists extended the soviet system of organization throughout Siberia, into Central Asia (Turkestan), and in the 

Caucasus region east of the Black

Sea, until, in addition to European Russia, they had control over one third of the continent of Asia. To govern a population of 139,000,000 people scattered over such an area required a new type of constitution. 

This was seen in the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics which was put 70 kon 70 

RUSSIAN STAMP 

Under the Communist régime. into effect in 1924. Five soviet republics in Europe and Asia were linked to the main Russian system at Moscow. A general congress of soviets composed of representatives from these republics and also from a number of autonomous districts within Russia is the supreme legislative body for the entire union. But actual power resides in the various committees and commissaries, all under the stern discipline of the 

Communist party leaders.

The Methods and Power of the Communist Party. The soviet system, whether in the union, in the individual republics, or in the autonomous districts, is a very complicated affair which would scarcely function at all if it did not have some directing force. This force exists in the Communist party, composed of

a few hundred thousands out of the millions of voters. The party determines in its caucuses upon the policies, foreign and domestic, of the state. It selects the editors of the authorized newspapers. It sends out its agents to influence the local soviets. 

Its members make up a special military force which is used by the political authorities to crush opposition at home, or to inculcate revolutionary doctrines in other countries. 

Evidence of the attempts of the Russian Communist party to overthrow other governments has been found a plenty. 

Through a University of Oriental Nationalities in Moscow it trains young people to stir up trouble in the existing colonies and states in Asia; a work which has been especially successful in China. It has its agents in every continent, and in 1927 brought down upon itself the antagonism of England, one of the first western states to recognize soviet Russia. Yet the need of 

Russia for the expert advice and manufactured goods of other nations has led the soviet government to temper its policy until the time arrives when Russia shall become economically independent. In the meantime she is using her raw materials and especially her foodstuffs to purchase from other nations machinery with which to build up her five-year plans for the future. 

Bolshevism Continues in Modified Form. - For many years the Bolshevist system continued, although its economic theories greatly impoverished the land, and although its boasted democracy is merely a substitution of the tyranny of the few for the tyranny of the czars. In 1921, however, the government substituted a food tax for the seizure of the peasants' crops. Later it also modified its system of public management and ownership of factories by giving leases to individuals and associations to operate many industrial plants. But, beginning in 1928, a reversion to extreme communism was apparent. Opponents were killed or exiled and the class of middlemen obliterated. Immense communal farms were established to take the place of the small peasant holdings, and the communistic experiment appeared in 1929 to be more thoroughgoing than ever before.

RADICALISM GIVES PLACE TO CONSERVATISM 

Early Radical Successes. - The close of the World War saw the old governing classes discredited in most of the countries of Europe. It was felt that their mismanagement of affairs had been the cause of the ruin and destruction of the past four years. 

Consequently, at the conclusion of peace, a wave of radicalism spread over Europe that at first drove the older leaders from power and replaced them by men of socialistic ideas. In Germany not only was the monarchy overthrown, but a socialist republic was even established with a saddle-maker, Ebert, as its first president. In Great Britain the Labor party came into power for the first time in 1923 with Ramsay MacDonald as prime minister, and undertook to direct British policy in the interests of the laboring men. In the same year a coalition of the socialist and radical parties in France forced the resignation of the president, Millerand, while the socialist Herriot (âr-ryð′) succeeded the conservative Poincaré as premier. In Italy, too, for several years after the war the extreme socialist leaders gained great power.

Reasons for Conservative Reaction.—The success of the more radical elements in western Europe was brief. Many causes contributed to discredit them in the eyes of the majority of the people. The restoration of normal conditions after the war was an extremely difficult matter and proved an impossible task in the hands of inexperienced officials drawn from the common people. To meet the interest payments on the gigantic war debts and to pay the rising expenses of government, most countries issued vast amounts of paper currency which sank steadily in value. The German mark, for instance, became completely worthless, while the French franc and the Italian lira shrank to less than one fifth of their original values. England succeeded in maintaining the value of her currency, but was confronted by the loss of much of her foreign commerce and by widespread unemployment of laborers, more than 2,000,000 men being out of work for a long period. The lack of success of the new democ-

RADICALISM GIVES PLACE TO CONSERVATISM 

803 racies in dealing with such conditions caused a reaction of sentiment in favor of the older theories of government. 

The chief cause for the distrust of radicalism, however, was the fear of Bolshevism. From the western point of view the 

Russian experiment in communism appeared a gigantic failure, and the people were alarmed at the Russian determination to carry their war against private property into every corner of the world. A conservative reaction, therefore, set in which drove from power many even of the more moderate socialists and restored the influence and authority of the middle and upper classes in most states. 

The Fascist Revolution in Italy. In Italy the Bolshevik propaganda had by 1921 succeeded in undermining the government to such an extent that all business was brought to a standstill. By a system of organized violence the radical leaders terrorized the timid officials and intimidated the police. They seized the railroads, interfered with the mails, and organized constant strikes in the factories in the hope of ruining the employers and forcing them to hand over the factories to the workmen. For a time it looked as if a "dictatorship of the proletariat " would be established after the pattern of Russia. The violence of the radical agitators, however, led to an equally violent reaction among their opponents, under the leadership of a remarkable man, Benito Mussolini (bā-ne'tō moos-sō-lē'nē). 

His followers were known as Fascisti (fä-she'stē) and were given a regular military organization. They were well-armed, wore black shirts as a uniform, and were placed under a rigid discipline with orders to attack the Bolshevik element in every community. In the civil war which followed, the Fascisti overthrew the radical element, who, as a last resort, ordered a general strike of all the workmen of Italy on August 1, 1922. Mussolini gave the government officials forty-eight hours to suppress the strike; and when they feared to act, the Fascisti took matters into their own hands, smashed the strike, and forced the workmen to resume work. Then, in October, 1922, the Black Shirts from all parts of Italy marched upon Rome and seized control of affairs.

The king was allowed to retain his crown, but Mussolini became dictator and absolute ruler of Italy under the official title of premier, though he was universally spoken of as "il Duce" (el doo'cha), or "the Leader."

So far, the Fascist régime in Italy has repudiated the democratic theory of government. It is an absolutism and, though claiming to be managed for the people, it is not controlled by the 

MUSSOLINI, DICTATOR OF ITALY 

people. The place of the old Italian parliament has been taken by a new body based upon a novel principle of representation. 

Instead of being elected by geographical districts, the members are chosen from special groups, such as teachers, bankers, trade unions, and employers. Even within these groups the Fascist party controls the nomination of candidates and their election. 

Under Mussolini Italy has shown herself domineering in her

RADICALISM GIVES PLACE TO CONSERVATISM 805 

foreign relations. Much to the alarm of other nations, she adopted a deliberate policy of expansion and of armament with a view to future wars. This was stated in Mussolini's speech of May 26, 1927, when he said: "It is a fundamental duty to perfect our armed forces. We must at a certain time be able to mobilize 5,000,000 men. We must be able to arm them. 

We must fortify our navy and make our air force so strong and numerous that its roaring motors will drown all other sounds, its shadows hide the sun over Italian soil." 

A noteworthy early accomplishment of Mussolini was the settlement of the controversy which for fifty-nine years existed between the papacy and the kingdom of Italy. By the terms of a treaty signed on February 11, 1929, the pope recognized the kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital. In return for this, the Fascist government conceded the full sovereignty of the papacy over the "City of the Vatican," a small district including St. Peter's and the Vatican buildings and gardens. The 

Italian state further agreed that the teaching of religion should be compulsory in all elementary and secondary schools; that canon, or church, law should be enforced throughout the country; and that the sum of $87,500,000 should be paid as a settlement of all papal claims against the kingdom. 

Conservative Reaction in Other Countries. - In no other country at this time did reaction against radical ideas go so far as in Italy. Such ideas, however, lost ground throughout central and western Europe. On the death of the socialist president of 

Germany, Herr Ebert, in 1925, the people elected as his successor General von Hindenburg, the most popular military figure of the war. While he was loyal to the new republic, his sympathies were with the upper classes who formerly ruled Germany. In 

Great Britain the Labor government lasted scarcely a year and was replaced in 1924 by a Conservative ministry under Premier Baldwin. Restored to power in 1929, it was again overthrown by a Conservative coalition in 1931. The socialist ministry in France gave place in 1926 to a cabinet headed by the stanch nationalist Poincaré.

THE WASHINGTON ARMS CONFERENCE OF 1921 

Differences between America and Japan. Not only had the war destroyed the naval power of Germany, but it had also greatly stimulated the building of warships by America, England, and Japan. With the return of peace, each of these powers was committed to an elaborate program of naval construction. Suddenly it was realized that a new naval race was on - Japan and the United States especially vying with each other in the number and power of their warships. 

This naval competition between the United States and Japan was especially dangerous since misunderstanding and suspicion already existed on both sides. Japan had never ceased to resent the treatment of the 111,000 Japanese immigrants among us. 

Our ownership of the Philippines, too, seemed a menace to Japan. 

Other points of irritation existed in the Pacific and the Far East. Japan was generally credited with being imperialistic, bent upon building up by force a great empire in the Pacific islands and in China. Color was lent to this suspicion by the annexation of Korea in 1910 and by the agreement forced upon China in 1915 which seemed to place her under the guardianship of Japan. Then at the Paris Conference of 1919 

Japan insisted that the former German concessions in the Shantung Peninsula should be granted fully to her, with only an oral understanding binding her to return the region to China. The 

Anglo-Japanese Alliance was unpopular in America,¹ and was likewise offensive to the British dominions, which saw in it a possible menace to their policy of admitting only white immigrants.²

represented were France, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, and China. The sessions began on November 12, 1921. 

Secretary Hughes, as chairman of the conference and as spokesman for America, presented a very definite program of naval limitations which thrilled the world by its frankness and courage. 

After ten weeks of thorough discussion, the Hughes plan, slightly modified, was adopted by the five maritime powers, Great Britain, Japan, France, Italy, and the United States. A naval holiday for ten years in the building of capital ships was to put an end to international rivalry. In total tonnage of major warships, Great Britain and the United States were to have equal strength, while Japan was to have three fifths the strength of either of these. Thus was established the famous 5-5-3 naval ratio for these three countries. France and Italy were each to rank a bit more than half as strong as Japan. The three leading powers promptly ratified the treaty for carrying out these agreements, and by August, 1923, all five had ratified. 

The Results of Naval Disarmament. - Most dramatic was the execution of the provisions of this naval limitation treaty, when noted battleships were given over to be scrapped, when vessels contracted for remained unfinished, and when shipyards were closed for lack of work. Yet the agreement left much undone. It did not limit the size or number of submarines; it placed no restrictions on any craft under 10,000 tons; and although it did limit the size and total tonnage of aircraft carriers it placed no other check upon aërial warfare. Thus the treaty, while restricting the size, armament, and number of battleships and heavy cruisers, actually encouraged greater competition in the building of smaller vessels, of submarines, and of airplanes. 

A Plan to Keep the Pacific Peaceful. A second agreement made at the Washington Conference to remove suspicion was known as the Four Power Pacific Treaty between America, Great Britain, Japan, and France. This treaty bound the four powers not to attempt "land-grabbing" from one another in the Pacific. In case of threatened friction between any two over conflicting interests, all four were to confer to adjust the matter.

THE WASHINGTON ARMS CONFERENCE 

809 A conference was likewise to be held in case the interests of one of the four in the Far East should be threatened by some outside power. The Anglo-Japanese Alliance came to an end upon the ratification of this Pacific Treaty in August, 1923.

99 1 Efforts to Safeguard China. - All of the nine powers represented in the conference joined in an important agreement concerning China, at that time torn and distracted by civil war. 

The powers all agreed to maintain in China the " open door."

None of the powers was to take any more land from China, or to gain control over her government, or to establish any new spheres of special influence, or to acquire any more leased ports. 

By a special agreement Japan promised to return to China the former German territory in the Shantung peninsula. 

1. Who first made this principle famous? How?

Why the Washington Conference Was Notable. All to gether, the Washington Conference seemed one of the most promising congresses in recent history. It was marked throughout by a spirit of fair play and confidence by each nation in the justice and chivalry of the others. A definite stop was put to the ruinous competition in the building of sea giants. China was, for a time, guarded against outside intrusion during her internal breakdown. It was clearly demonstrated that nations are capable of reaching a high plane of right dealing and idealism through the coöperation of men of reason and good will. 

THE VILLAGE AND ABBEY OF LONGPONT, FRANCE, IN 1918 

The conference, moreover, removed the attitude of mutual suspicion and distrust which was then threatening the friendly relations of the United States and Japan. Shortly afterward 

Japan carried out her agreement by returning in 1922 the Shantung Peninsula to China.

However, Japanese intrusion in China was resumed about ten years later, as we shall see farther on. 

TRYING TO MAKE THE TREATY OF VERSAILLES WORK The Reparation Problem Proves Knotty. - The territorial changes provided for in the peace treaties were fairly well carried out except in the case of Turkey,' but the other articles of the

MAKING THE TREATY OF VERSAILLES WORK 811 

treaties were more difficult to enforce. The efforts to collect from Germany reparations for the destruction of the lives and property of civilians proved the greatest task of all. 

The Interallied Reparation Commission under the Treaty of Versailles was to fix the amount of the German debt to the Allies and to supervise its collection. After careful study, the commission set 132,000,000,000 gold marks 2 as the amount Germany was to pay, and arranged a plan of payment extending through thirty-six years. From the signing of the treaty in 1919, Germany had been making some payments on account, partly

in gold and partly in kind - coal, cattle, lumber, etc. - all grudgingly and slowly. Meanwhile, at a conference during 

1920, the premiers of the Allied countries decided upon the basis of distribution of the expected reparations. France was to receive 52%; England, 22%; Belgium, 8%; Italy, 10%; 

Serbia, 5%; and others, 3%. Because of the special ruthlessness of the devastations in Belgium, that country was to get her share first.3

But progressively the German payments dwindled. This was in the face of the fact that Belgium and France were restoring the devastated areas at their own expense by means of heavy taxes and additions to their own national debts. The Allies,

This occupation, for fifteen years, had been authorized by the treaty of Versailles, Germany paying the cost of occupation.5

France and Belgium Occupy the Ruhr Valley. In spite of 

English objections, France and Belgium thereupon sent their armies into the Ruhr Valley. This region, east of the Rhine, was the very heart of the industrial life of Germany, with its rich coal mines and its great centers of iron and steel manufacture. 

In disapproval of the occupation of the Ruhr, the United States forthwith called home from Coblenz the small American army which had been stationed there since the armistice of 

November, 1918.

In occupying the Ruhr Valley the French maintained that their aim was not annexation. All that they desired, they announced, was to be able to collect taxes from German industry, to force the delivery of coal due under the treaty, and to hold a sort of mortgage on Germany's business life until she was willing to meet her obligations squarely. But Germany declared the occupation a violation of the treaty, resisting for months, largely passively, the authority of the French officers, and continued to print more paper money until it became utterly worthless. 

The Dawes Report Points the Way Out. Gradually the pressure of France and Belgium began to tell upon Germany. 

In 1923 Germany ceased resistance in the Ruhr and showed a willingness to reach an adjustment. Then, early in 1924, an international commission of financial experts, headed by Charles G. Dawes, an American, presented a notable report which seemed to point the way out of the tangle. 

The commission reported that Germany was able to pay reparations which by 1928 ought to reach a standard rate of 2,500,000,000 gold marks yearly. How this could be done, how business prosperity could be restored in Germany, and how a sound national currency could be reëstablished, the report

pointed out so fairly that Germany, as well as the creditor nations, announced a readiness to try the Dawes plan (1924). 

Within a few months Germany had established a new sound currency and was making her required reparation payments. 

In August, 1925, France and Belgium evacuated the Ruhr district, as agreed. In 1929, a more liberal schedule of payment was provided for by an international conference headed 

Wide World Photos CHILE HOUSE, HAMBURG, A MODERN GERMAN SKYSCRAPER 

by an American, Owen D. Young, for whom the plan was named. But the world-wide depression following 1929 furnished a cause, either real or assumed, for Germany's refusing the regular reparation payments. In 1931 Germany defaulted; in June, 1934, she even refused to pay interest on the public and private loans so generously made to her by the Allies.

France and Germany Settle their Differences. The most encouraging sign of future peace in Europe was the set of agreements reached by France, Germany, and other powers in a conference held at Locarno, Switzerland, in October, 1925, under the leadership of Briand of France and Stresemann of Germany, the foreign secretaries of the two countries. France, Belgium, and Germany agreed that the Rhineland boundaries as fixed by the Treaty of Versailles should be inviolable; that they would never invade one another's territory, and never again resort to war against each other. Any differences whatever arising between them were to be settled by arbitration. Great 

Britain and Italy agreed to act as guarantors of this treaty, that is, their influence and force would be used against any one of the three nations which should be found to be in the wrong. 

Special arbitration treaties were also entered into between Germany on one side and Belgium, France, Poland, and Czechoslovakia, individually, on the other. And France also signed treaties with the two last-named states, guaranteeing them security from attack by Germany. On the part of Germany the acceptance of the Locarno treaties was conditioned upon her receiving a permanent seat in the Council of the League of Nations. Accordingly, on September 10, 1926, the German delegates took their place beside the representatives of Great Britain, France, Italy, and Japan, as entitled to permanent seats in the Council; while the elective seats were increased to nine, making the total Council membership fourteen. 

The Locarno pacts marked a great advance toward universal peace in the period 1918-1925. They took the Rhineland countries (Alsace-Lorraine) out of the realm of international dispute; they seemed to array the major force of western Europe on the side of right against an aggressor; they brought, for several years, security in place of fear and dread; they adopted the principle of international arbitration; and, for Germany, they brought an end of isolation and an honorable place in the European councils. With cheerful optimism the whole civilized world rejoiced in this project for banishing war.

Interallied Debts Cause Ill Feeling. During the World 

War England and the United States, and in a much less degree France, were able to furnish munitions, military supplies, and food for the use of the other combatants allied against Germany. 

Even after the armistice of November, 1918, very considerable quantities of goods were advanced to the weaker Allied nations and even to some of the enemy countries to aid in restoring their normal industrial life. Such supplies usually were not given outright to the other nation, but were represented by debts which, it was believed, might be paid off after victory was gained. 

Expressed in dollars, the sum of these debts was enormous. 

Great Britain's advances to her allies amounted to over ten billion dollars; the American loans equaled about the same figure; and, in the latter case, by 1927 these debts represented over half of our national debt. Could such huge debts ever be paid? Was it just that peoples which had suffered so severely during the actual fighting should be saddled with the repayment of money advanced to them by the richer countries? 

Naturally the European states would have been willing to cancel all such debts among themselves if the United States would cancel the large sums owed to her by the various countries. 

All would benefit by such an arrangement except the United States, which owed no one. To such proposals the American 

Congress has turned a deaf ear. It has held that the debts are legally payable to us, and if they are not paid by the debtors they must be met by taxes on the American people to provide for the Liberty Loans when they fall due. Consequently the American government insists that the debts be recognized and some arrangement for payment be arrived at. Up to January, 1930, settlements had been made by Belgium, Great Britain, Italy, France, Poland, and a number of the lesser states. France, of the great debtors, was the last state to make definite provision for what she owed the United States. In arranging for the payment of the debts the American World War Foreign Debt Commission has applied the principle of considering the capacity to pay of each debtor nation. The payments have been spread

MAKING THE TREATY OF VERSAILLES WORK 817 

considering the capacity to pay of each debtor nation. The payments were spread out over sixty-two years, and both the principal sums and interest rates were reduced, the terms varying with the economic resources of the several countries. 

The capacity to pay, however, was greatly reduced by the economic depression following 1929, and it presently became evident that the agreements made by the debtor countries with the United States would not be entirely fulfilled. The first break in the arrangements came in the spring of 1931 when Germany announced her inability to make the payments required under the Young plan of 1929. The imminent national bankruptcy of Germany menaced the finances of all other countries. So, to avoid a world catastrophe, President Hoover proposed a year's moratorium, or suspension, not only on the payment of German reparations but on the payment of all inter-allied debts. Since then no arrangement satisfactory to the European countries and the United States has been worked out. Some of the debtor countries were in default in 1932, and nearly all defaulted in 1933-1936, bringing the total arrearages to more than a billion dollars, and made no plans for a resumption of payments. Only little Finland, with its semiannual installment of $166,000, met its obligations in full; the other nations paid little or nothing of the amounts due. How much, if anything, will be paid on the remainder of those debts — totaling over $10,000,000,000 - will depend upon the mutual temper of the debtor states and of the American Congress. 

The League of Nations at Work. - Membership in the 

League of Nations fluctuates a little from year to year. Up to 

June, 1936, sixty-two countries had been members, the United States being the only important nation which has never joined. 

Several states have withdrawn, including Costa Rica, Brazil, Japan, and Germany. The League has settled problems of disputed boundaries which might have brought on war. Until the Saar district by popular vote rejoined Germany on March 1, 1935, the league conducted the affairs of that region; it still assists in the government of the free city of Danzig; and it

has some jurisdiction over 30,000,000 persons of minority races in various countries, and over the inhabitants in the regions mandated by the peace treaties. The elaborate provisions of those treaties have placed a great burden upon the league. 

The League Works to Prevent War. The carrying out of the terms of the peace treaties is only a temporary part of the league's activity. The authors of the league covenant hoped that the main work of the organization would be to prevent all war in the future. They wished to bring about a general disarmament and to establish a will for peace. Undoubtedly the league has helped at times to promote a feeling of national security among the nations, but it has had no real influence in reducing armaments, which were greater in 1937 than in 1913. 

Although the league has signally failed in direct measures for disarmament, it has discouraged war by its policy of publicity. 

Diplomacy has been made more open, the meetings of the Council and Assembly are closely observed, and the publication of all treaties lessens the fear of secret alliances. 

In controversies between Sweden and Finland, and between Greece and Bulgaria, the league was successful in preventing war. In the quarrel between Bolivia and Paraguay it succeeded only in delaying but not in preventing their war of 1932-1935. 

In 1935, also, the league failed in its attempt to prevent war between Italy and Ethiopia in east Africa.

The World Court to Settle Disputes among Nations. 

war was to be abolished some other method of deciding conflicts among nations had to be found, and this was provided for in the league covenant by sections relating to arbitration and to the judicial settlement of controversies. Out of these provisions has grown the World Court or "Permanent Court of International Justice," established under the auspices of the League of Nations, but not controlled by it. The court was organized in 

1922 with eleven judges, one of whom, John Bassett Moore, was an American. It is a continuous body like our Supreme Court, ready at any time to try international cases of a legal nature. 

Its first case was decided in 1923, and since then it has passed

819 judgment upon a number of cases, some of which if not settled peaceably might have caused serious international trouble. 

The United States had been vitally interested in the Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907 and it was active for many years in obtaining arbitration treaties with other nations. So, too, Americans like William H. Taft, Elihu Root, John Bassett 

Moore, and James Brown Scott had been at work for years in promoting a permanent international tribunal, and our citizens P&A Photos 

THE COUNCIL OF THE LEAGUE OF NATIONS 

A view taken during the first sitting after the Council was enlarged to a membership of fourteen. had even had a share in outlining the organization of the new World Court. Yet the United States has not joined the other powers who promise to submit their differences to that court. 

In January, 1926, the United States Senate agreed to the court plan but accompanied its acceptance with five reservations designed to protect American rights and to prevent our being drawn into obligations respecting the European states. These reservations were not accepted by the other nations. In 1931 new terms were proposed, generally considered to be satisfactory, but our Senate put off final action. In this case, as in the matter of joining the League of Nations, a large number of Americans feel

that we must not surrender the advantages of our political and geographical separation from Europe. 

The Kellogg Treaty, 1928. The American sentiment in favor of the peaceful settlement of international differences found expression in a treaty proposed by the United States to other countries in the spring of 1928. This "Kellogg pact,' named after the American Secretary of State, is a very brief statement of general principles. As signed at Paris, August 27, 1928, by representatives of fifteen nations, the treaty condemns recourse to war in the solution of international controversies; renounces war as an instrument of national policy; and promises that the parties to the treaty shall seek the settlement of international differences solely by pacific means. The treaty was duly ratified and was formally proclaimed in effect in July, 1929. 

Nearly all the nations of the world have joined in this treaty. 

The London Naval Conferences. In 1930 representatives of the United States, Great Britain, Japan, France, and Italy met in London to discuss naval disarmament. While the conference was not as successful as its friends had hoped, some progress was made by an agreement which placed limitations upon the number and armament of war vessels under 10,000 tons, which were not regulated at all at the Washington Conference (see page 808), and upon the size of submarines; it also made rules for saving the lives of noncombatants on ships attacked by submarines. This agreement gave hope that a future naval competition might be avoided among the three chief maritime powers, Great Britain, the United States, and Japan. Such hopes were shattered by the action of Japan. She remained dissatisfied with the earlier arrangement of the Washington Conference limiting the size of her navy to the ratio of 3 to 5 as compared with the navies of the other two powers. Another naval conference in London at the end of 1935 failed to continue the work of the two previous meetings. Japan insisted on the equality of her navy with that of any other country, denounced the 5 5 3 ratio, and withdrew from the conference in January, 1936, thus starting a new race in the building of warships.

MAKING THE TREATY OF VERSAILLES WORK 821 

The League Promotes International Coöperation. 

In many ways the League of Nations has encouraged coöperative undertakings among nations and individuals. In the field of public health it has had remarkable successes, by noting the existence of epidemic diseases, by checking their spread from the point of origin, and by studying means for their prevention. By the interchange of health officers of various countries it has placed the experience of each at the disposal of others. The league, too, has been studying means for the international control of the trade in opium and similar drugs. 

Much other humanitarian work has been directed by the league, of which perhaps the most notable was the return to Greece of more than a million refugees from Asia Minor, who were settled in useful occupations within Greek territory. Hundreds of thousands of other refugees- Bulgarians, Poles,

Turks, Armenians, and others have been distributed in regions where they may work happily side by side with the people of their own nationality. 

All forms of international activity are fostered by the league, whether among individuals, organizations, or nations. A bulletin published quarterly by the league describes some 360 such organizations, many of which are of a scientific or charitable character. At Geneva, the seat of the league activities, there now center a great many of those coöperative enterprises which tend to bind the world together. In such undertakings Americans take part in promoting an era of better feeling in the world. 

IMPORTANT RECENT EVENTS 

The world-wide

Hard Times Cause New Political Unrest. 

business depression which began in 1929 affected the political life of all countries. In times of economic depression people are inclined to hold the government responsible for bad conditions; and when other causes of political unrest are also present, the way is prepared for revolution, as we have seen in the Europe of 1848 (pp. 340-341). No such widespread disturbances occurred in Europe in 1929-1930, but economic distress

had much to do with the wave of revolution which swept over large parts of Latin America in 1930 and 1931. Existing governments were then overthrown by force, though without much bloodshed, in Argentina, Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Guatemala, and Panama.

Trouble in Spain. - Spain in the nineteenth century was considered one of the most backward countries of Europe. 

Spanish Liberals blamed this on the monarchy, which was accused of maintaining the semifeudal conditions of the seventeenth century by bestowing undue favors on the church and the great landowners and by opposing all reform. In recent years Spanish Liberals were supported by a strong Socialist party, likewise hostile to the monarchy. Republican sentiment finally grew so strong that in 1931 King Alfonso XIII was forced to flee the country, and a republic was established there. 

The new republican government, controlled by moderate Liberals, attempted to carry out many reforms, in particular the distribution of the great landed estates of the nobles and the church among the poorer peasants. The victory of the conservative elements in the elections of 1934 put an end to the reform program; but in March, 1936, a combination of the 

Liberals and Socialists with the growing Communist party again placed the reformers in control of the government. This combination of parties, however, quickly broke up. The more moderate elements failed to satisfy the Communists, who proceeded to throw the country into great disorder by strikes and riots. 

The result was an armed revolution of the reactionary elements, which began in July, 1936. The revolt, headed by 

General Franco, was supported by most of the regular army, by the church, and by the landed proprietors. To these were added the warlike Moorish tribesmen of North Africa and large contingents of Italians and Germans, while many liberal sympathizers from Russia, France, and elsewhere joined the government forces. The Spanish civil war, the most ruthless and destructive of modern times, was still being waged in the autumn of 1938.

IMPORTANT RECENT EVENTS 

823 Recent Events in Germany. - The German people felt humiliated by the Treaty of Versailles- the loss of all their colonies; the loss of various districts in Europe inhabited chiefly by Germans; enforced disarmament; and, most of all perhaps, compulsory acceptance of sole blame for the late war. 

Their resentment led to the growth of an intense feeling of nationalism, which found expression in the rise of a new political party, the National Socialists - shortened to Nazis in popular speech. After 1931 this party grew rapidly under the fiery leadership of Adolf Hitler. 

Owing to the many political groups in the country, no party or combination of parties was able to control the Reichstag, and parliamentary government broke down because of the political confusion. In January, 1933, after much agitation, President von Hindenburg named Hitler chancellor, as the Nazi party was the strongest of the twelve parties then in the Reichstag. In the following election the Nazis won almost as many seats as all the other parties combined. At Hitler's request the Reichstag promptly transferred its powers to him and adjourned, thus making him dictator of Germany. On the death of von Hindenburg in the summer of 1934, all the presidential powers were also transferred to Hitler by popular vote, and he took the title of 

Fuehrer, or Leader, of the nation.

A policy of extreme nationalism was carried out by the Nazis. 

The Jews, as a people of alien race, were excluded from the higher life of the nation and practically deprived of all rights of citizenship. The full training of German youth was taken over by the 

Nazis in order to instill their principles into the rising generation. 

Finally, the new government practically repudiated the Versailles treaty. It denied responsibility for the war and declined to make further payments of indemnities. It fully rearmed the nation by again introducing universal military service and by building a strong navy and an immense air force. 

In January, 1935, the people of the Saar, who had been separated from Germany and placed under control of the League of Nations by the treaty of 1919, were allowed to express their

desire as to their future status. By a majority of 9 to 1 they voted to be reunited to Germany and were accordingly restored to that country. In 1936 the new German army reoccupied the strip of territory along the Rhine which had been set aside by the peace treaty as an unfortified zone, and proceeded to fortify that entire frontier. The reoccupation of the Rhineland, together with the rearming of Germany, started a new armament race in Europe more violent than in the period before the World War. 

The old Austrian empire had been broken up at the end of the World War (see page 777). Its most purely German section was set up as the little state of Austria, weak and almost defenseless. In March, 1938, Hitler led a German army into Austria and annexed the state to the German Reich, thus bringing most of the German people of central Europe under a single government. Hitler also demanded the border lands of Czechoslovakia, where lived about three and a half million Germans, called Sudetens. After controversies and negotiations that narrowly averted another European war, the Nazis took possession of several of these border districts in October, 1938. Czechoslovakia also yielded smaller districts to Poland and Hungary. 

The Five-Year Plans in Russia. The Bolshevist system, as we have seen (page 800), underwent certain modifications from time to time. Late in 1928 it was boldly announced that 

Russia would be made completely communist within five years. 

This meant that privately owned farms would be merged into great collective areas worked by tractors, reapers, and other agricultural machinery, and that the peasant would be turned into a wage-earner like the factory worker. It meant that the petty industries of the country would be grouped into immense factories, turning out clothing, iron, steel, automobiles, electric energy, and all the other things which a progressive state might need. It meant that the independent farmer or merchant would be wiped out, and all industrial organization would be on a communistic basis, with the state owning everything and assigning to each worker what it thought he needed.

IMPORTANT RECENT EVENTS 

825 In December, 1932, Dictator Stalin announced that the objectives of the five-year plan had been accomplished in four and a quarter years. A second five-year plan was at once announced, to be devoted largely to producing ordinary articles needed by the people rather than heavy capital goods. Though the condition of the people is still, from an American standpoint, extremely wretched, their standard of living is improving. Even some of the luxuries of capitalistic countries can be obtained by the fortunate few, such as good clothing and even powder and lipstick for young women. Wages higher than the average are being paid to the more fortunate workers, and a privileged class is gradually coming into existence, though now based on the importance of the worker rather than upon birth. Family life is being fostered by discouraging divorce, and the pattern of Russian life is growing more like that of other countries. 

Economic progress, however, is retarded by great military expenditures for defense against a possible war with Japan and Germany, both bitterly hostile to communism. 

Manchuria. Efforts to preserve Chinese territory intact (page 810) proved in vain. The weakness and lack of unity among the Chinese furnished too great a temptation to Japan, with her rapidly growing population and her poverty in natural resources. The northeast provinces of China, known as 

Manchuria, were rich in fertile farming lands as well as in coal and iron, and contained a population of nearly 30,000,000. 

A small proportion of these inhabitants were Japanese immigrants who had either settled on the land or built up great mining and manufacturing industries. Claiming the right to protect her citizens and to guard the Japanese-built railroads in Manchuria against attacks of Chinese bandits, Japan drove the Chinese troops out of Manchuria in September, 1931. 

China appealed to the League of Nations, which attempted to intervene to preserve Chinese territory, but without success. 

The military party in control of the Japanese government refused to modify its policy. For the sake of appearances Manchuria was organized as a so-called independent state, called

Manchukuo. It was placed under the former boy-emperor of 

China, who was, however, maintained only by Japanese arms and entirely controlled by Japanese advisers. Thus Manchuria was torn away from Chinese sovereignty. 

Not satisfied with Manchukuo, Japan desired the economic and political control of the whole of China. Chinese efforts to maintain independence led to a Japanese invasion in July, 1937, with the destruction of many cities, the killing of vast numbers of the civil population, and the plundering of the survivors. By the autumn of 1938 the Japanese armies had occupied most of northeastern, and much of central, China without crushing the spirit of the people or forcing the Chinese government to submission.

Italy Annexes Ethiopia. - Italy, in the Treaty of Versailles, was denied a share in the German colonial empire. Her resentment was frequently expressed, and Mussolini prepared to enlarge Italy's possessions in some other direction as soon as European politics should tie the hands of other countries. His opportunity came when the rearming of Germany in 1935 filled the French with alarm at the possibility of another European Moved by these fears, France refused to antagonize Italy and thus make a new enemy. Hence she was willing to give only half-hearted support to the League of Nations, the only defense of weaker states against the aggression of the strong. war.

Mussolini's ambitions were directed toward Ethiopia (Abyssinia), one of the two parts of Africa still free from European control. Though a half-civilized land, it possessed a recognized government under an emperor, and was a member of the League of Nations. Therefore, when the Italians sent an army to invade the country, the emperor appealed to the League for protection. 

That body attempted in vain to arrange a peaceable settlement; but France refused to support strong measures. The Italian armies invaded Ethiopia in October, 1935, and seven months later the emperor fled into exile. On May 9, 1936, the annexation of the whole country was announced, and the King of Italy was proclaimed Emperor of Ethiopia.

The British Crown Changes Heads. The Silver Jubilee of 

King George V of Great Britain, in 1935, marking the twentyfifth year of his reign, demonstrated the monarch's great popularity among all classes. On his death the following year the 

Prince of Wales succeeded to the throne as Edward VIII. The new king showed signs of intending to play a more active part in public affairs than had his father, and, though extremely popular among the poorer classes, aroused some apprehension in conservative circles by his active interest in the unemployed. 

When he further showed his independence by indicating his intention of marrying an American woman who was then applying for a divorce from her former husband, the Conservative Prime Minister Baldwin opposed the marriage on the ground that it would tend to lower the prestige of the monarchy and was therefore a matter of government concern. Rather than yield to his ministers in this personal matter, King Edward abdicated the throne on December 10, 1936, and was succeeded by his brother, the Duke of York, as King George VI. 

The New Diplomacy of 1938. -The British prime minister, 

Neville Chamberlain, in several visits to Germany in September, 1938, conferred personally with Hitler, and later also with the French premier and with Mussolini, to avert a general war over the Czechoslovakian crisis (page 824). It was expected by many that international relations in Europe, no longer controlled by the League of Nations, would be dominated thenceforth by a four-power accord of the British, French, German, and Italian governments.
