CONCLUSION  AND AN APPRAISAL OF THE PRESENT 

A Small Fragment of World History. Now that you have finished studying the preceding chapter, with its varied glances over world affairs, you will probably want to look backward over the period of time covered in this book. And you will notice, first of all, that only a very small portion of man's history is discussed in this volume. How long indeed man has existed on the earth we do not know; but scientists believe he must have been here several hundreds of thousands of years. And this book, after a brief introductory portion, gives careful study to the course of human history for the last one hundred and fifty years, only a minute fragment less than one thousandth of the entire course of history. 

Yet to us these few years represent what is most important in our life today. We take for granted that some early men invented tools, tamed animals, and adopted a written language. 

We know that before written history began there were looms for weaving cloth and potter's wheels for making bowls and dishes. In very ancient times man knew the stars in the heavens; he was acquainted with the rudiments of mathematics; he installed irrigation systems; he had a belief in supernatural deities; and he had some form of political government. All of these things we take for granted. So, too, we accept as having a deep influence upon our lives such things as Greek and Roman civilization, the Christian Church and its doctrines, and medieval life and customs. We know that the 

Renaissance and the Reformation made a lasting impression upon all time. 829

But after all has been said about the significance of these great historic movements, there remains the feeling with most of us, that the nineteenth century, with its prelude in the eighteenth and its postlude in the twentieth, is the real formative period of modern history. Here we find the great movements which today powerfully affect our lives - Nationalism, Democracy, Industrialism, and Imperialism. Out of the conflict of these movements came the World War and the many results which have flowed from it. 

Nationalism in the Nineteenth Century and Today. Nationalism has been defined on page 294 as a feeling or sentiment which makes the people of one group, such as Germans, Poles, or Italians, consider themselves different from all other people. 

It urges them on to attain political independence and to unite in one state all people having similar national traits. 

In 1789 the thirteen American states were united under our Constitution and founded a union that was somewhat weak, but advancing rapidly in national spirit. In 1830 Webster had claimed that the federal union was a "copious fountain of national, social, and personal happiness." The War of 18611865 next broke down the theory of secession and led to a still stronger spirit of union and nationalism. From 1865 onward the United States was foremost among the national states, its people deeply imbued with patriotic impulses and caring little for what the rest of the world was doing. 

Somewhat similar to the progress of the United States toward nationalism was the revolt of the Latin-American states from Spain and Portugal, and the erection on the American continents of many independent countries. These new states were intensely patriotic, and they did not hesitate to engage in wars with their equally nationalistic neighbors. 

In Europe, modern nationalism has its origins in that uprising of the peoples against Napoleon which finally brought about his downfall. A period of repression followed, but soon all of 

Europe broke out in a blaze of nationalism. About 1830 the spirit of local independence led to the freedom of Belgium from

NATIONALISM 

831 Dutch rule, and of Greece from the despotism of the Turks. 

Everywhere people were studying their old national languages, recounting stories in the lives of their nation's heroes, and organizing groups, usually of young men, to achieve independence. 

There were Young Ireland, Young Italy, Young Hungary,

Young Poland, and many similar groups, all reaching out for the union and independence of their countries. Germany and 

Italy were the two most marked successes in the attainment of political unity in the nineteenth century. 

As the century advanced, the spirit of nationalism became more and more intense, often resulting in wars or threats of war among the nations of Europe. Indeed, the rivalry among the nations was one of the causes of the World War. 

Nationalism did not disappear in the World War; indeed, it was rather encouraged by President Wilson's insistence upon the self-determination of peoples. By this he meant that each race or people should have the right to its own form of government, and should have the right to be independent of outside control. Today with many new states formed in Europe, we see the results of this policy. The Baltic states - Finland, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland - are the direct creation of the war. All of them are today seriously imbued with nationalistic sentiment which seems to the people so essential to real independence. In the southeast of Europe we have the new states of Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, and Albania, made up respectively of north Slavic peoples, south Slavic peoples, and the ancient peoples inhabiting the lands west of Greece.

In other parts of the world, also, the doctrine of self-determination is rife, resulting in political upheavals and the establishment of new independent or semi-independent states. The 

Irish Free State now is a self-governing part of the British Empire; Egypt has achieved almost complete independence; 

India is still seething with discontent and entertains the hope of Indian government managed by the Indians. The Philippines have been promised self-government; the Dutch East 

Indies have a measure of local rule; the Arabians are struggling

. 

toward independence; while Manchuria, a great outlying province of China, is now governed, under Japanese compulsion, as the supposedly independent state of Manchukuo. 

It is evident that nationalism is anything but dead today. 

Actually the sense of narrow patriotism and the jealousy of other states is overwhelming, and colors the outlook of most peoples on international affairs. The future, which President 

Wilson had dedicated to the League of Nations, seems none too bright. In fact, an exaggerated nationalism is threatening the peace and prosperity of the world. The world of today needs broad-minded citizens, frankly loving their own country, but ready also to see the good in others. In these days of depression, with each one striving for the material satisfaction of his own wants, the need of a broad, liberal idealism is especially urgent. 

Democracy, Another Product of the Nineteenth Century. — 

The rule of the people, democracy as distinguished from absolutism or aristocracy, — is the political ideal toward which almost all the states of the world were tending in the nineteenth century. It is expressed in Jefferson's phrase in our Declaration of Independence, that "all men are created equal"; and it is seen again in the French Rights of Man, with the slogan "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity." Napoleon himself, while an arrant despot, yet helped the course of democracy by overthrowing feudalism and by granting civil rights to the people of the countries he conquered. After his downfall the pendulum swung away from democracy toward aristocracy as advocated by Metternich. But this did not last long. The United States had by this time granted the suffrage to nearly all men. was the country of opportunity for all. Here the "downtrodden and oppressed" of Europe could seek "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." No wonder that America should have its effect upon Europe, and that the political ideal of manhood suffrage should be the goal of various European revolutions. 

Great Britain, under her liberal constitution, was the first to advance toward democracy, and, after half a century of struggle, nearly reached that ideal. France followed in 1848 and again

DEMOCRACY 

833 In 1875, putting the suffrage upon a manhood basis. Similar action was taken in the last half of the century by Italy and by Spain. And in the same period nearly all adult males were given the right to vote in many of the smaller states, such as 

Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Portugal.

In other parts of the world the same ideals were reached in the British self-governing colonies, in South America whenever the dictators could agree to it, and in the American colonies of the Philippines and Hawaii.

Some countries of Europe gave lip-service to the democratic ideal while their practice was far removed from that goal. 

Germany and Austria-Hungary had complicated systems of voting which nullified the ostensible right of each man to a vote. 

Russia, Turkey, and the Balkan states surrounded the suffrage with such residence, property, or tax-paying qualifications that it was not worth while for a common citizen to attempt to cast his ballot. The same respect for the western European pattern of elections, but without its real value, was seen in the Japanese suffrage act of 1908, which gave only 33 per cent of the population the right to vote. "To make the world safe for democracy" was the ideal of many participants in the World War. The first result of the war, therefore, was seen in a great extension of the suffrage in 

Russia, Turkey, Germany, Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia,

Yugoslavia, and the smaller states. In many cases not only manhood suffrage was obtained, but woman suffrage as well was introduced. A movement begun by American women in 

1848 had spread to other countries and by 1920 the most important nations, except France and Italy, had granted to women the same suffrage provisions as those already given to men. 

Under the arrangements for fair and impartial elections which were generally adopted it seemed as if the world had at last reached a safe harbor for democracy. But, as we shall see later on (pages 840-843), political democracy in many countries has given place to dictatorships, whose autocratic ways are enough to make Woodrow Wilson turn in his grave.

Advancing Industrialism of the Great States. The world of today has become mechanically-minded. We push a button and our house is illuminated; we push another button and we are thrilled with radio music or bored by radio jazz or lectures; we turn a switch and our automobile or airplane rushes us through space at marvelous speed; on every hand are devices which perform in a moment operations that formerly might have occupied hours or days or even months. The age of steam seemed wonderful to our predecessors, but its marvels are puny indeed compared with those wrought by electricity and its applications to the radio, to the movie, and to transportation, power, and lighting.

The Industrial Revolution began in England. In a generation it had reached America; another generation saw it traveling across Belgium, France, and the Rhine region. By the close of the nineteenth century it had awakened the people of Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy, and even had invaded Russia. 

Wherever the Industrial Revolution came, it brought immediate prosperity to the factory owners, to those that controlled the new machinery. It led to a great increase in the amount of goods produced; it cheapened the price and made available to all classes many articles which even kings had lacked in earlier days.

But it had its disadvantages. A large portion of workers in the old hand industries could not easily adapt themselves to the routine of factory life. The older men and women whose muscles were hard and set from laborious operations could not learn the new processes. The nimble fingers of young people and of children were better suited to the delicate machinery installed in many manufacturing establishments. Unable or unwilling to accept the discipline of factory rules, the old folks were as wrecks on the sea of life, unacquainted with the new charts and unfamiliar with the new types of management. 

Their day had passed. Each new machine was a labor-saving device which occasioned new unemployment, and down to our own time the process has continued. Fortunately, today the

INDUSTRIALISM; IMPERIALISM 

835 workers are more intelligent and are better able to change their habits as changing industries direct. 

Factory workers at first worked long hours at very low wages and with little opportunity for pleasure or enjoyment. Philanthropists at length rebelled against this misery of their fellows and insisted that steps be taken to modify the harsh features of the factory system. Beginning with England - for the 

Industrial Revolution had begun there factory legislation spread to other countries until today it is almost as widespread as the factory itself. Such legislation limits the hours of labor in factories, mines, and other establishments; it provides for the protection of the life and health of employees; it regulates, in many cases, the minimum wage that shall be paid. 

In general, the laborer today is in a far better position than he was when factories first began to change our industrial life. 

Instead of working twelve or fourteen hours a day, he now has, in some countries, only six or eight hours, with Sundays and often Saturdays free of all required labor. His wages are far above those of earlier days, and governmental bodies see to it that these wages are upheld. He is surrounded by conveniences and even comforts furnished by the industry itself. The worker may, or may not, yet have the full share of his reward in industry, but in times like those of the recent depression, he can see that government has done what it could to keep his position safe and secure.

Imperialism as a Factor in Modern Life. The growth of industry created a great mass of goods more sometimes than could be consumed by the home country. Consequently manufacturers looked to foreign markets for an outlet for their surpluses. People said that "trade follows the flag." They believed that a country could not be great or prosperous without colonies. Such colonies would furnish the place where raw materials might be produced for the home country, and where manufactured goods could be sold to the backward peoples. 

Thus a new race for colonies began. Great Britain, which held many colonies throughout the nineteenth century, was in

a most favored position. She possessed colonies not only in the temperate regions of North America and South Africa, but also in the tropical regions of both hemispheres. Her wideflung empire was self-contained, producing almost every possible form of raw materials and of manufactured goods. France came rather late into the colonial field, yet she controlled northern Africa, large sections of central Africa, some Pacific islands, and Indo-China. The Dutch, dating back to their contest with Spain and Portugal in the sixteenth century, owned a large area of tropical islands in the East Indies. 

Germany and Italy achieved national unity toward the close of the nineteenth century. They came late into the colonial field, and they were never successful colonizers. Italy acquired various stretches - mainly desert on the north and northeast coasts of Africa. Bismarck, in Germany, at last realized the significance of colonies and looked about for some to annex to his empire. German acquisitions were made in Africa, in certain islands of the Pacific, and in spheres of influence in China. 

But at best Germany's colonial world was scattered, it was inhabited by tribes little used to commerce, and it did not contain the basis for a great empire. 

The United States, also, came late into the race for colonies. 

The Spanish-American War brought the Philippines and Puerto Rico to our country, and at about the same time we annexed Hawaii and several other islands in the Pacific. Imperialism, however, never became a real feature of our policy. We trained our colonies for self-government, either under American auspices or, in the case of the Philippines, for complete independence. 

Rivalries among the Great States Lead to War. - The colonial and industrial jealousies of the states of Europe were further emphasized by military and naval rivalries. When 

Great Britain's two-power navy- that is, a navy greater than those of any other two powers-was threatened by Germany's building of a greater fleet, the British took alarm. They expended larger and larger sums on their navy in order to keep well ahead of their rival. When Germany increased the number of men in

RIVALRIES LEAD TO WAR 

837 her army, France felt compelled to do likewise. Hence the concert of Europe was anything but harmonious. The Triple 

Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy was opposed by the Triple Entente of Great Britain, France, and Russia. 

The smaller countries of Europe, especially those in the Balkan region, looked on like jackals ready to pick up some of the scraps after the lions had fought it out. 

It happened, however, that the jackals fell first to quarreling among themselves. The Balkan wars of 1912-1913 did not settle anything finally. But they aroused such enmity that they led on toward the greater contest of 1914. 

The World War was a great trial of the strength of the contending groups of nations (page 749). On many occasions it seemed as if the Central Powers would win the war. Thus in the autumn of 1914 the Germans were within a few miles of their objective, Paris, the fall of which might have meant the conquest of France. Again in 1916, under the leadership of the Crown Prince, German armies nearly broke through the French line at Verdun. Finally in the spring of 1918, after 

Russia had withdrawn from the war and Italy had been badly defeated, the Germans launched a series of great attacks upon the western front, hoping to separate the French and British armies, seize the Channel forts, and compel a victory before the Americans could come to the aid of the Allied forces. 

But American troops, crossing over the Atlantic on "the bridge of boats," reached France in greater and greater numbers each month. Over two million Americans had been ferried across by November, 1918. These troops, fresh in the vigor of young manhood, who did not know what fear meant, and whose cry was "On to Berlin," brought new hope to the war-weary peoples of England, France, and Italy. It was their might and strength, added to the reviving spirits of the Allies, which won the war. 

The Allied nations could not alone have conquered Germany; neither could the Americans alone have crushed the enemy; but the coöperation of the two brought the final victory. The welding together of the Allies and Americans for war purposes

was a foretaste of that international coöperation which Wilson prophesied would produce the League of Nations. 

Significance of the World War. - Many wars in history have seriously modified the course of events in the states involved. 

A nation might be defeated; it might be conquered; its existence might be blotted out by the victorious party. But generally such results of previous wars were local, affecting only one nation so seriously. Never before in the history of the world were the consequences of a war so widespread as those that followed the contest of 1914-1918. Several nations, as you know (pages 776-777), suffered severe losses of territory; several made gains of territory; several nations gained independence under newly created governments; and a League of Nations was organized, soon to be joined by most of the countries of the world. 

On the human side alone, the results of the World War were astounding. Sixty millions of men were called to arms in the countries involved, and of these one sixth were killed and nearly the same number permanently disabled. More civilians died of disease, starvation, and privation than were killed in the war. 

Perhaps you can visualize such losses by noting that they numbered as many as the entire population, in 1920, of the states of Texas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Arkansas, all eight of the Plateau States, and all three of the Pacific States; and that the permanently disabled numbered as many as the 1920 population of Pennsylvania!

On the money side the losses were almost inconceivable. They added up to 338 billions of dollars, a sum far in excess of all the wealth, real and personal, of the United States in 1918. The countries engaged in the war entered deeply in debt to their own citizens and to other nations to the amount of 260 billion dollars. 

They owed on this figure many billions every year in interest. 

They also obligated themselves to pay other billions to the widows and children of their dead soldiers, and to the living disabled veterans.

Yet these were not the only costs of the war. Immediately after the Armistice on November 11, 1918, millions of people were

EFFECTS OF  

839 starving because of the failure of crops, the absence of means of transportation, and the political chaos which ruled in many European regions. It is very much to the credit of the United 

States that we took over a great share in alleviating the distress in the war-stricken countries. Several years after the close of the war, also, American relief was given in Armenia, Greece, and Turkey; and in 1921 in Russia, where a serious famine swept off five millions of the population. Many more must have died had it not been for American help. We well may be proud of our aid in these acts of charity and helpfulness. 

The Influence of the War upon Politics. - President Wilson had said in 1917 that the war would make the world safe for democracy. It remained to be seen how far such a doctrine would succeed. After the close of hostilities, democracies were established in Germany, in Austria, in Czechoslovakia, in Poland, and in some of the other states which succeeded to the older monarchies. These democracies had a broad, liberal suffrage, with the vote open to all men and women. The legislature and the executive officers were chosen by ballot. Other democratic features, almost socialistic in their tendencies, were provisions for the assignment of the land to actual farmers, the national control of electric and power utilities, and the national regulation of railroads and other industries. The ideal of democracy seemed about to come true. 

But the countries of Europe were facing very serious economic problems, which simple arrangements for democratic government could not, in many cases, solve. Currency was being inflated until in Germany and Russia it took millions or billions of the nominal unit to buy a loaf of bread or a postage stamp. 

Industry was not reviving in the way people thought it would. 

Taxes, raised to excessive heights during the war, were not and could not be reduced; while their amount tended to restrict the renewal of business enterprises. The various nations, also, were jealous of one another; they levied high tariffs on products of their neighbors to prevent their crossing the borders, and they actually threatened war in order to gain their aims.

AN APPRAISAL OF THE PRESENT 

Further complications were introduced by the Russian Soviet system of government, and by the despotism adopted by the Red leaders. They were anxious to overthrow the existing type of industry in other countries as well, and to put in its place a socialistic state which would operate and control all forms of agriculture and manufacturing. Patterned on the Russian model, such Soviet organizations existed for a time in Bavaria, Hungary, and Italy. Under these circumstances many people turned from democracies and supported dictatorial government, which ruled without control of legislature or popular vote. 

The Age of Dictators. The period through which we are now passing became in many lands an Age of Dictators. While government by arbitrary rulers had not reached Great Britain or France, few other European countries, near the end of 1934, were free from the directing hand of the despot. 

Russia, first under Lenin, and then under Stalin, has been absolutely controlled by the Communist chief. This ruler is the head of the Communist party, the small group of about two million persons who govern the other one hundred and fifty millions in the Soviet state. The Communists are in charge of the agricultural tractor stations; they manage the vast electrical and manufacturing plants; they control the railroads. In the movies, in the theater, in the schools and universities, in the press, and in art the Communist authority is dominant, directed when necessary by Stalin himself. Here is a dictatorship in an extreme form. Adequate safeguards for the citizen accused of crime do not exist. Suspects are arrested by the secret police in the dead of night; they are tried without redress; and they face exile to Siberian wastes. Some are even condemned to death for crimes which would not be considered misdemeanors in other countries. The "dictatorship of the proletariat" is not a democratic form of government, but a genuine despotism under the control of one man Stalin. 

In Italy another type of dictatorship has arisen since the war, known as Fascism. The name refers to the small groups of agitators bound solemnly together in much the same fashion as

THE AGE OF DICTATORS 

841 the fasces of the old Roman lictors were tied together into a fagot of rods. In practice Fascism absolutely controls the government of Italy, and seeks to embody all social institutions, such as the family, the church, the school, and the trade union, in the "totalitarian" state under its control. Its support came first from the agricultural classes, who are, in Italy as in Russia, mostly opposed to Communism; and secondly, from the middle class of clerks and skilled workers, small merchants and shopkeepers, mechanical experts, and members of the professions.

To these groups may be added the greater number of those who were loyal to the monarchy. Fascism is opposed to Communism, and entered into a deadly contest with that faction in the north of Italy. It is opposed also to the parliamentary system of the democratic countries; it rejects universal suffrage; it believes that government can best be managed by a small body of experts, selected not by popular vote but by the choice of the 

Fascist leaders, especially by Benito Mussolini.

Fascism in Italy is largely the creation of Mussolini. His fiery eloquence aroused in the people, particularly in the young people, the desire to achieve fame under their leader. He has always advocated the dangerous life, and he tells his followers, "If I advance, follow me; if I retreat, kill me; if I fall, avenge me!" Emotional, almost unthinking obedience to the national leader (the Duce) is the ideal of Fascism. Under the Fascist rule the state controls the education of youth, training the young men in the ideals of the party and getting them ready for compulsory military service. It controls the press by forbidding the publication of articles, papers, and books in opposition to the state. It controls industry and agriculture by organizing the workers and employers into corporate units, and by imposing upon both parties the observance of special contracts. Thus 

Italy is ruled by a dictator, who, with his party of about one million Fascists back of him, directs the state and all its concerns. 

The dictatorship is different from that of Russia, yet the dominant will in each is that of a personal despot, carrying out his own wishes for what he thinks is the welfare of his country.

AN APPRAISAL OF THE PRESENT 

Still another despotism has lately been established in Germany, where the republican constitution has been overthrown, and its place taken by the will of the national leader (the Fuehrer), Adolf Hitler. The new German ruler is a fiery speaker whose impassioned oratory made many converts to his cause. Like 

Mussolini, Hitler is supported by those who are opposed to Communism and yet possess no faith in republican representative institutions. A leader who denounced the Versailles treaty, who refused to make payments on account of reparations, who demanded the return of former German colonies, who advocated union with Austria, and upheld the right of Germany to arm itself such a leader would naturally gain a following. To these proposals which affected the foreign policy of his country, Hitler added the idea of the unity of all Germans, members of the Nordic race, and the refusal to allow Jews to become citizens or to occupy positions of political, economic, or social importance. 

In March, 1933, Hitler induced the Reichstag to give him dictatorial powers for four years. The death of President von Hindenburg in 1934 removed all checks to the dictator's authority. 

Strongly intrenched in power by the almost unanimous votes of the Reichstag and the German people, Hitler rules the country with an iron hand. The regulations of war time have been put in force, with strict censorship of newspapers and books, with the rationing of foodstuffs, clothing, and household effects, and with continued persecution of the Jews. The policy of Hitler in 1934-1938 was nationalism of the crudest type; and it pointed toward foreign wars. those of Russia,

Three dictatorships have been mentioned Italy, and Germany - but it must not be supposed that these are the only despotisms today. If we put on one side the democratic states of France, Great Britain, and the Scandinavian countries, and all the remaining European states on the other side, we shall find that nearly all of the latter are now being governed, or have recently been governed, by dictators. Poland and the Baltic states have submitted to government by certain individuals, each of whom may have at heart the real interests

WHERE ARE WE GOING TODAY? 

843 of his country, but whose methods are those of the despot. 

Turkey, under its new régime, has prospered under a dictator; 

Hungary has an "authoritarian" government, that is, a nearly absolute government by executive authority; Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, and Rumania also have endured - and perhaps prospered under such governments. 

Where Are We Going Today? The world, indeed, is now passing through a period of change, in which mankind is seeking, under varied forms of government, to attain to the rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. There is no doubt at all that these individual rights can best be preserved under the democratic form of government. While the dictatorship may give prosperity to some of the citizens, yet its very form has within it the seeds of arbitrary rule and of later dissension. 

Always in the past such despotisms have succumbed before the attacks of other groups in the state. 

The United States, and other countries as well, need a practical man's government, possessing the power to make quick decisions in important matters affecting the interests of the citizens, and yet retaining ultimate control by the people, and individual rights for all. Under such a government, with a spirit of unselfishness on the part of the citizens, we may again be sure that the American union remains a fountain of happiness. We believe that America can lead the world toward true democracy that democracy which, when functioning properly in the hands of tried and intelligent officers, gives the best promise for the future of the world.
